content: LIGHT, also referred to as tumor necrosis factor superfamily member 14 (TNFSF14), is a secreted protein that belongs to the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) superfamily. It is recognized by herpesvirus entry mediator (HVEM) and decoy receptor 3. The name LIGHT stands for homologous to lymphotoxin, exhibits inducible expression, and competes with HSV glycoprotein D for binding to herpesvirus entry mediator, a receptor expressed on T lymphocytes. In the cluster of differentiation (CD) nomenclature, it is classified as CD258. The protein encoded by this gene is a member of the TNF ligand family. It serves as a ligand for TNFRSF14, a receptor that is part of the TNF receptor superfamily and is also known as herpesvirus entry mediator ligand (HVEML). LIGHT may act as a costimulatory factor for the activation of lymphoid cells and as a deterrent to herpesvirus infection. It has been demonstrated to stimulate T cell proliferation and induce apoptosis in various tumor cells. Additionally, LIGHT has been reported to prevent TNF-alpha-mediated apoptosis in primary hepatocytes. Two alternatively spliced transcript variants encoding distinct isoforms of this protein have been identified. LIGHT has been shown to interact with several proteins, including TNFRSF14, TNFRSF6B, BIRC2, TRAF2, and TRAF3. In the context of herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection, LIGHT plays a role similar to how CD4 functions as the primary receptor in HIV infection. HSV glycoprotein D (gD) binds to the HVEM receptor, which is also required by TNFSF14/LIGHT. This binding reduces LIGHT's ability to activate the NF-κB pathway. NF-κB is a survival factor that inhibits apoptosis by triggering a pathway that suppresses caspase-8 activity. When HSV gD binds to HVEM, LIGHT is non-competitively inhibited from binding, which promotes apoptosis in the infected cell.
